learning_outcomes.text: Knowledge in basic and technological subjects, enabling them to learn new methods and theories, and providing them with versatility to adapt to new situations.
Knowledge of atomic structures and their defects and ability to control material properties by modifying atomic structures with defects.
Knowledge of the magnitudes that define the different properties characterizing the behavior of industrial materials.
Knowledge of phase diagrams that enables them to fluently handle binary equilibrium diagrams and the fundamentals of ternary diagrams.
Knowledge of the fundamentals of materials science, technology, and chemistry. Understand the relationship between microstructure, synthesis or processing, and the properties of metallic materials.
Ability to design heat treatments to modify the microstructure and properties of steels, cast irons, and non-ferrous alloys.
Ability to use diverse materials and combine them appropriately to design composite materials with controlled properties.
Ability to solve problems with initiative, decision-making, creativity, and critical reasoning.
Basic knowledge of concepts related to product verification and inspection and ability to handle specifications, regulations, and mandatory standards.
Identify the structures of fundamental crystalline solids and assess the importance of different structural defects.
Interpret the different properties of materials and also be able to determine them experimentally using appropriate testing techniques.
Interpret equilibrium diagrams and use them in material development.

Fluently handle the Fe-C diagram, transformation curves, evaluate the influence of alloying elements in these products, the practical use of Jominy hardenability curves for steels, and the effects of heat treatments.
Discern the main characteristics of industrially important non-ferrous alloys that justify their application, assess the importance of alloying elements, and the effects of heat treatments.
Differentiate between the different families of plastic materials, ceramics, and composite materials, their main characteristics, advantages, and limitations for industrial use.
Ability to define the fundamental characteristics that describe crystalline structures.
Ability to use diffusion laws for various calculations.
Ability to determine the conventional mechanical properties of industrial materials by conducting corresponding experimental tests.
Ability to determine electrical, magnetic, thermal, and optical properties from experimental methods.
Ability to interpret binary equilibrium diagrams and to locate points and determine the phases present in ternary diagrams.
Ability to interpret the Fe-C diagram and the transformation curves of steels and cast irons to modify their microstructure and properties through mechanical and heat treatments.
Ability to prepare metallographic specimens, perform heat treatments, and interpret the microstructures of iron-based materials.
Ability to interpret the base equilibrium diagrams of the most important non-ferrous metallic alloys and use them to define their characteristic heat treatments.
Ability to handle and interpret equilibrium diagrams in ceramic systems and to control their properties from their manufacturing processes.
Ability to interpret the mechanical properties of plastics based on their structural characteristics and manufacturing processes.
Ability to calculate the properties of composite materials from those of their constituent simple materials.
Foster in the student a curiosity for the acquisition of scientific knowledge.
Lay the foundations for the student to be able to apply the acquired knowledge in engineering.
Formation of an open, critical, and entrepreneurial spirit.

syllabus_topics: PL 1. Crystallography. Metallographic preparation and grain size determination.
PL 8. Microstructures of steels and cast irons.
PL 10. Non-ferrous metallic alloys and ceramics.

assessment_methods.method: Submission of proposed exercises (mandatory for continuous evaluation)
Attendance to all laboratory practices and submission of completed guides
Final exam (continuous evaluation) - Laboratory practices part
Final exam (continuous evaluation) - Theory and exercises part
Final exam (non-continuous evaluation) - Laboratory practices part
Final exam (non-continuous evaluation) - Theory and exercises part
Final exam (differentiated evaluation) - Laboratory practices part
Final exam (differentiated evaluation) - Theory and exercises part

assessment_rules: For continuous evaluation, the final grade is calculated as: (P1+...+P5) + L + 0.65*EF, where P1-P5 are partial exams (max 3 points), L is lab grade (max 0.5 points), and EF is the final exam score out of 10, weighted at 0.65. A minimum score of 4 out of 10 is required on the final exam, with at least 30% in each of its three parts, and the overall grade must be 5 or higher. For non-continuous and differentiated evaluation, there is a final exam consisting of a lab practices part (1 point) and a theory and exercises part (9 points); a minimum score of 5 and 30% in each of the three parts is required to pass.
